extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates in algebraic geometry (Math 216 students)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository and exercise material on maps between projective schemes (Proj), rational and birational maps, representable functors, group schemes, and the initial construction of the Grassmannian. Includes definitions, propositions, examples, and exercises used to check/construct these objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-definedness of projective maps via homogeneous polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: A map CP1 → CP2 given by [s,t] ↦ [s^{20}, s^9 t^{11}, t^{20}] is well-defined because replacing (s,t) by (λs,λt) yields the same point in CP2: the three coordinate polynomials are homogeneous of the same degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that all coordinate polynomials are homogeneous of the same degree; this guarantees the map descends to projective space. The example emphasizes verifying homogeneity to conclude well-definedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic correspondence: maps of graded rings induce maps of Proj (opposite direction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism between projective schemes Proj S• → Proj R• is induced by a graded ring homomorphism R• ← S• given by specifying images of generators that respect degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret geometric maps in terms of maps of graded rings in the opposite direction; verify degree considerations and the hypotheses (e.g., hypothesis (6.4.0.1)) needed for the ring map to induce a morphism of Proj.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis for graded ring maps to induce Proj morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a technical hypothesis (referenced as (6.4.0.1)) on a graded ring homomorphism φ : S• → R• (e.g., conditions about images of S+ generating R+ or related) that must be satisfied for the induced map on Proj to be defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify algebraic hypotheses on φ (for instance that φ(S+)R = R+ or analogous conditions) to ensure the map of graded rings gives a well-defined morphism Proj R• → Proj S•; exercises suggest checking equivalent algebraic formulations (see Exercise 6.4.B and hints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proj is insensitive to finitely many degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: Different maps of graded rings can give the same morphism of schemes; if two finitely generated graded rings R• and S• differ only in a finite number of degrees, then Proj R• ≅ Proj S•.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why constructions that alter only finitely many graded pieces do not change the associated Proj; exercises (6.4.C, 6.4.F) ask to show precise statements. Use this when simplifying or regrading rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of nth Veronese subring and its effect on Proj
rubrics_metrics.description: For a graded ring S•, the nth Veronese subring Sn• := ⊕_{j≥0} S_{nj} (regrading by taking 'old degree' n to be 'new degree' 1). The inclusion Sn• ↪ S• induces an isomorphism Proj S• ≅ Proj Sn•.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When f ∈ S+ is homogeneous of degree divisible by n, distinguished opens D(f) correspond under the isomorphism; exercises (6.4.D, 6.4.G) guide checking how distinguished opens cover Proj and how regrading helps assume generation in degree 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generation in degree 1 preserved under Veronese
rubrics_metrics.description: If S• is generated in degree 1, then Sn• is also generated in degree 1; conversely, after taking a suitable Veronese subring one can often reduce to the degree-1 generated case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Exercise 6.4.E and 6.4.G: find a d so that Sd• is generated in ('new') degree 1; this is useful to reduce to the common hypothesis that graded rings are generated in degree 1 when embedding Proj into projective space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regrading to assume generation in degree 1
rubrics_metrics.description: By taking appropriate Veronese subrings (regrading, keeping only degrees that are multiples of d and dividing degree by d), any finitely generated graded ring can be replaced by one generated in degree 1 for the purposes of Proj.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 6.4.G combined with 6.4.D shows there is little harm in assuming degree-1 generation; this simplifies embedding and representability arguments (used later to embed Proj into projective space).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of rational map
rubrics_metrics.description: A rational map X ↛ Y is a morphism defined on a dense open subset U ⊂ X (i.e., a morphism f:U→Y) considered up to the equivalence that two such morphisms agree on some dense open subset of their intersection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rational maps are 'morphisms defined almost everywhere'; keep track of representatives and equivalence relation. The text warns to avoid calling a rational map simply a 'map' to prevent confusion with morphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational maps of S-schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: For S-schemes X and Y, a rational map is defined similarly but with representatives being morphisms of S-schemes on dense opens; definitions must respect the S-structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working relative to a base scheme S, ensure all dense opens and morphisms are S-morphisms; examples and results about rational maps extend to this context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant rational map
rubrics_metrics.description: A rational map π:X↛Y is dominant if for some (hence every) representative U→Y its image is dense in Y. For irreducible schemes this is equivalent to sending the generic point of X to the generic point of Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Exercise 6.5.A to check equivalence for irreducible schemes. Dominance is the geometric analogue of injectivity on function fields (maps of function fields go opposite direction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of (dominant) rational maps
rubrics_metrics.description: Dominant rational maps compose: if π:X↛Y is dominant and ρ:Y↛Z is a rational map, then ρ∘π is a well-defined rational map; if ρ is dominant, the composition is dominant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing representatives, restrict to appropriate dense open subsets where maps are defined. This allows formation of a category of integral schemes with dominant rational maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maps of function fields vs rational maps
rubrics_metrics.description: Dominant rational maps of integral schemes induce morphisms of function fields in the opposite direction. Conversely, under finiteness hypotheses (integral finite type k-schemes) maps of function fields preserving k induce dominant rational maps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful: maps of function fields do not always correspond to rational maps in general (counterexample: Spec k[x] vs Spec k(x)); Proposition 6.5.7 gives a sufficient finiteness condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Birational map and birational equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: A rational map π:X↛Y is birational if it is dominant and admits a rational inverse ψ that is also dominant, with compositions equivalent to identities. Two reduced schemes are birational iff they have dense open subschemes that are isomorphic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as the notion of isomorphism in the category of integral schemes with dominant rational maps; Proposition 6.5.5 gives the equivalence via existence of dense opens U⊂X, V⊂Y with U≅V.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a rational variety over k
rubrics_metrics.description: An integral finite type k-scheme X is rational if it is birational to affine space A^n_k for some n (i.e., its function field is purely transcendental over k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should make precise the compatibility of the structure map k→K(X) with the isomorphism K(X) ≅ k(x1,...,xn); Exercises (e.g., 6.5.D) discuss categorical equivalences relating varieties and function fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: constructing dominant rational map from extension of function fields
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is an integral k-scheme and Y is an integral finite type k-scheme, and φ♯:K(Y)→K(X) is a k-preserving inclusion of function fields, then there exists a dominant rational map φ:X↛Y inducing φ♯ (Proposition 6.5.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: shrink to affines X=Spec A, Y=Spec B generated by y_i, express images as fractions in K(A), clear denominators to get a map on some localization A_g → B, yielding a morphism on an open subset. This is a standard way to produce rational maps from field maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domains of definition of rational maps extend over regular codimension 1 points (foreshadow)
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurring theme: domains of definition of rational maps to projective schemes extend over regular codimension-1 points; this is made precise in the Curve-to-Projective Extension Theorem (16.5.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show extension phenomena (e.g., conic parametrization extends over a point); be aware of limits when the codimension-1 set is singular (examples illustrate failure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using projection from a rational point to parametrize conics (Pythagorean triples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a rational point p on conic C: x^2+y^2=1, projecting from p gives a birational map C↛A^1 (coordinate m = slope), yielding parametrizations x=(m^2−1)/(m^2+1), y=−2m/(m^2+1) and a method to produce Pythagorean triples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This geometric method is an explicit construction of a birational map; check where the rational map is defined and whether it extends (exercise shows extension over p in this example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Care with maps of function fields not always giving rational maps
rubrics_metrics.description: Although dominant rational maps induce maps of function fields, the converse can fail without finiteness hypotheses: e.g., Spec k[x] and Spec k(x) share function field k(x) but there is no rational map Spec k[x]↛Spec k(x) of k-schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always verify existence of a ring map from an open subset's coordinate ring to the target ring; finiteness conditions (finite type) are important to obtain rational maps from field maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representable functor concept and h_Y
rubrics_metrics.description: For a category C, the contravariant functor h_Y defined by h_Y(X)=Mor(X,Y) represents maps to Y. A contravariant functor F:C→Sets is representable if F ≅ h_Y for some Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret representability as identifying an object Y that parametrizes the data F(X). The bijection Mor(X,A^1) ≅ Γ(X,O_X) is the motivating example showing the global sections functor is representable by A^1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global sections functor represented by A^1
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural bijection Mor(X,A^1) ≅ Γ(X,O_X) (maps to affine line correspond to global functions), and this bijection is functorial in X (natural isomorphism of functors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to motivate representability; check functoriality diagrams commute as in §6.6.2. Exercises (6.6.A, 6.6.1) ask to verify and apply this bijection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of representing objects up to unique isomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: If a contravariant functor F is represented by Y and also by Z, then there is a unique isomorphism Y ≅ Z induced by the natural isomorphism of functors (Exercise 6.6.C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a standard universal property argument (Yoneda-style); use it when identifying moduli-like objects to show the representing scheme is unique up to unique isomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmation: affine n-space represents the functor of n functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The contravariant functor X ↦ {(f1,...,fn): fi ∈ Γ(X,O_X)} is represented by A^n (Exercise 6.6.E(a)); likewise, invertible functions are represented by Spec Z[t,t^{-1}] (G_m).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit coordinate functions on A^n to establish the universal property; gives concrete representing schemes for familiar functors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the multiplicative group scheme G_m
rubrics_metrics.description: The scheme Spec k[t,t^{-1}] (or Spec Z[t,t^{-1}] over Z) is the multiplicative group G_m; it represents the functor taking X to invertible global functions Γ(X,O_X)^×.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: G_m is the standard example of a representable group-valued functor; exercises ask to check group operations and representability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of group object and group scheme axioms (categorical formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A group object in a category C with final object Z and products is an object X with morphisms m:X×X→X (multiplication), i:X→X (inverse), e:Z→X (identity) satisfying associativity, identity, and inverse axioms expressed by commutative diagrams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate usual group axioms into categorical diagram commutativity; checking these diagrams in Sch yields the notion of a group scheme. Exercises (6.6.G–6.6.K) guide constructing and verifying these maps for A^1 and other examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group scheme: group object in category of schemes (or A-schemes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A group scheme is a group object in Sch; a group scheme over a ring A (or scheme S) is a group object in the category of A-schemes (or S-schemes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: A^1 with suitable maps, G_m, GL_n, SL_n (kernels of determinant), µ_n; exercises discuss representability of kernels and subtle nonreduced phenomena in positive characteristic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functoriality of group schemes: Mor(X,G) inherits group structure
rubrics_metrics.description: If G is a group scheme, then for any scheme X the set Mor(X,G) inherits a group structure functorially; pullback preserves group structure so Mor(-,G) is a functor to Groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Exercise 6.6.H to check the group axioms are preserved under composition; this viewpoint forces the categorical definitions of group objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine group schemes correspond to Hopf algebras
rubrics_metrics.description: If G = Spec A is an affine group scheme, the group object structure on G corresponds dually to algebra maps on A giving it a Hopf algebra structure (comultiplication A→A⊗A, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a standard equivalence: express categorical axioms for the group scheme in terms of co-operations on the coordinate ring; Exercise 6.6.T suggests writing the Hopf structure for Z[t].

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and patching description of the Grassmannian G(k,n)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Grassmannian parametrizes k-dimensional subspaces of an n-dimensional free module; it is covered by affine 'Schubert' patches U_v ≅ A^{k(n-k)} given by expressing a k-plane as the span of vectors in a chosen basis in row-reduced form, and patches are glued along opens where certain determinants don't vanish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe coordinates a_{ji} on each patch, impose normalization (a_{ji}=δ_{ji} on pivot columns), and glue via change-of-basis matrices; Exercise 6.7.B guides the explicit gluing and determinant conditions for overlaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two bases are related by invertible matrices (gluing condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any two bases of A^⊕n are related by an invertible n×n matrix over A (i.e., a matrix with determinant an invertible element of A); this fact underlies the transition maps between Grassmannian patches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use that invertible change-of-basis matrices parametrize the overlap maps; the nonvanishing of certain minors/determinants describes where a given patch covers the Grassmannian and where gluing occurs (Exercise 6.7.A/B).
